job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Vera Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in manufacturing engineering at Millbrook Technical University, and I live with my parents above their shop, which sells phone repairs and accessories. Most days I'm in the workshop lab measuring how a part wears, or in the library writing up results. My bachelor's was in mechanical engineering, and I finished top of the year, with a summer at a pump factory and a placement at a car parts supplier. For my final project I redesigned a gearbox housing so it was cheaper to cast. I do my own calculations and drawings, and I've never used an AI tool, because I like knowing where my numbers came from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, things stay steady. I'd tell my classmates that machines don't get built by chatbots and that factories still need engineers who can stand next to the machine. I wouldn't make a big deal of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm relieved, but I'm not carefree. Pump factories have been closing in parts of the region, and the one I interned at laid off 40 people last winter. I worry about finding a job near home, not about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, apply to eight or nine manufacturers within a two-hour drive, and keep working Saturdays in my parents' shop. I'd ask the foreman at the pump factory, Mr Kowalczyk, whether they'd take graduates again. I'd keep my savings, about 1,500, where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly steady, a bit tense about the local market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a layoff last winter. What do you remember about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The engineers who stayed were the ones who knew the machines, which made me proud and also scared. A friend of mine on the quality team lost her job after eleven years. It wasn't AI, it was an order that went abroad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if no local job appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd consider a job two hours away, but I'd hate leaving my parents with the shop. My mum's knees are bad and my dad can't lift the stock alone.

say: Machines still need **engineers** who can stand next to them.
I'd keep calm and wait for **steady** hiring.
think: I'm relieved, but **local factories** are already closing, and one laid off 40 people.
My real worry is finding a **job near home**, not robots.
do: Apply to **eight or nine** manufacturers within two hours' drive.
Keep working **Saturdays** in my parents' shop.
Ask Mr Kowalczyk whether the pump factory takes **graduates**.
feel: **Steady**, a bit tense about the local market.
S0.quote: The engineers who stayed were the ones who knew the machines, which made me proud and also scared.
fieldNote: Vera's unease in the mildest scenario comes from **local factory closures**, not from AI.
She is tied to home by her parents' **shop**, which limits how far she'll look.

steps.text: Apply to eight or nine manufacturers within two hours' drive
Work Saturdays in my parents' phone repair shop
Finish the master's and keep my 1,500 savings untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mostly an office problem at first. Drafting, checking and planning get easier, but you still need someone who can read a worn part and know why it failed. I wouldn't say that too loudly, because I'm not sure I believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm anxious. A lot of what I do as a junior is calculation, drawing checks and cost sheets, and those are the exact tasks software takes. Firms might hire fewer of us and ask the ones they hire to do more, and I'm slow to take up new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take an evening course in CAD automation and, reluctantly, try one AI tool on a past project to see where it fails. I'd widen my search to include maintenance and quality roles, where a person with hands and eyes still matters. And I'd ask my old tutor, Dr Brandt, for two more references.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but sensible about it. It's a push to do what I've been putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're slow to take up tools. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like to understand how a thing works before I trust it. With these tools I can't see inside, and that bothers me. With a calculator it's easy, you can check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it showed its working, like a hand calculation. And if my supervisor trusted it first and took the blame if it failed. I'm not brave about that.

say: The office work gets easier, but you still need someone who can read a **worn part**.
I'm not sure I believe my own reassurance, though.
think: Calculations and **cost sheets** are what junior engineers do, and software takes them.
do: Take an evening course in **CAD automation**.
Try one AI tool on a past project to see where it **fails**.
Widen my search to **maintenance** and quality roles.
S1.quote: I like to understand how a thing works before I trust it. With these tools I can't see inside, and that bothers me.
fieldNote: Vera's resistance is not stubbornness: she wants **traceable working** before she trusts a tool.
She expects fewer **junior roles** and sees maintenance and quality as a safer path.

steps.text: Take an evening course in CAD automation
Try one AI tool on my gearbox housing project to see where it fails
Apply for maintenance and quality engineer roles near home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't know what to say. In two years, most of my firm's office would be replaced, and the shop floor would hold for three more years. I'd tell people that the government needs to be honest about this and not pretend it'll sort itself out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm scared. The design and calculation jobs I trained for would go first, and all that top-of-the-class work would feel like it was for a world that ended. My parents' shop sells phone repairs, and that could be automated too eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the idea of the master's if it isn't leading to a job, and apply for hands-on roles right away: maintenance technician, commissioning, installing machines. I'd put every spare coin in the bank, about 200 a month from my shop wages. And I'd ask my dad whether we could add a repair service for small appliances at the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit numb. It's too big to picture, so I think about the next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd leave the master's. What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would cry, then cook for a week. My dad would say 'do what's practical.' He never finished school and he'd be proud of me getting a practical job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Hands-on work has about three more years. What do you do with them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a trade certificate in industrial maintenance and become the person who looks after the robots. If a robot breaks, someone with a spanner has to know why.

say: The government needs to be **honest** and not pretend this will sort itself out.
I honestly don't know what to **say**.
think: The design and calculation jobs I trained for would go **first**.
My top marks would feel like they were for a **world that ended**.
do: Drop the master's if it isn't leading to a **job**.
Apply for **maintenance**, commissioning and installation roles.
Get a trade **certificate** in industrial maintenance.
feel: **Anxious** and a bit numb, because it's too big to picture.
S2.quote: If a robot breaks, someone with a spanner has to know why.
fieldNote: Vera's idea of safety is **physical**: the person who maintains the machines when thinking AI has taken the desk.
Her feelings go numb at this scale, so she plans in **months**, not years.

steps.text: Get a trade certificate in industrial maintenance
Apply for commissioning and machine installation roles
Save 200 a month from shop wages
Suggest adding small appliance repair to my parents' shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to see the signs. I'd say employers should hire graduates now and train them, rather than waiting. I'd also say we need a clear plan for what schools teach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm anxious, but I'd have a job and a record by then. By 2031 I'd be 29, with five years in a factory or plant, and I'd know the systems from the inside. That's better than being new, but it's still not safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first manufacturing job I'm offered and move up to production engineering. I'd save about 250 a month and pay down the loan, about 9,000. I'd also take a course on industrial control and robotics, because the hands-on shift in 2034 is when my job changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but with a plan. Five years is a stretch of road I can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes between two years and five for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have time to learn the robot side while I'm still being paid. In two years I'd be starting cold. The extra three years are worth more than the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there something you'd miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the chance to just be a graduate and enjoy the work. I'd be learning constantly. I'm tired already, and I'm 24.

say: Employers should **hire graduates now** and train them, not wait.
Schools need a clear plan for what to **teach**.
think: By 2031 I'd have a **job and a record**, which is better than starting cold.
do: Take the first **manufacturing job** and move up to production engineering.
Save **250 a month** and pay down the 9,000 loan.
Take a course in industrial **control** and robotics.
feel: **Anxious** but with a plan, because five years is a stretch of road I can see.
S3.quote: The extra three years are worth more than the money.
fieldNote: Vera values **time to learn** robotics on the job more than any salary.
She admits she is already **tired**, so the cost of constant learning is real to her.

steps.text: Take the first manufacturing job offered and aim for production engineering
Save 250 a month and pay down the 9,000 loan
Take a part-time course in industrial control and robotics

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to prepare if people actually do. I'd tell friends to pick a trade skill alongside their degree. I'd also say not to panic, since many predictions about technology have been wrong before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be uneasy rather than scared. By 2036 I'd be 34, perhaps with a family and a mortgage, and I'd have a decade of practical experience. The 3 years after, when robots arrive, still worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, build a career in production engineering and pay off the loan in four years. I'd keep helping with the shop, and maybe buy a small share in it. And I'd learn to use the tools slowly, a year after others, once I trust them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not a feeling that stops me sleeping, just one that stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use the tools later, once you trust them. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, yes. I'd rather be second and right than first and wrong. In two years it wouldn't be an option.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want your life to look like at 34?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A flat of my own near my parents, a steady job, and a Sunday where I'm not worried. That's honestly all.

say: Ten years is enough to prepare if people actually **do** it.
Many tech predictions have been **wrong** before, so don't panic.
think: I'd be **uneasy** rather than scared, with a decade of experience.
The three years after, when **robots** arrive, still worry me.
do: Finish the master's and pay off the **loan** in four years.
Keep helping with the **shop**, maybe buy a small share.
Learn the **tools** slowly, a year after others.
feel: **Uneasy**, not a feeling that stops me sleeping but one that stays.
S4.quote: I'd rather be second and right than first and wrong.
fieldNote: Vera's resistance becomes a **method** here: she adopts tools late but deliberately, once trusted.
Her goals are modest and **close to home**: a flat near her parents and a calm Sunday.

steps.text: Pay off the 9,000 loan within four years of working
Learn AI design tools a year after colleagues, once trusted
Buy a small share in my parents' shop
Build a career in production engineering at one plant

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because I'd have no job and no record when the desk work goes. What would help is training paid for while I learn, firms being asked to keep taking graduates, and clear information on which jobs last.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm a quiet person, and people assume I'm fine because I don't complain. I'd like someone to ask me what I'm afraid of before the plan is made.

headlineQuote: I'm a quiet person, and people assume I'm fine because I don't complain.
portrait: Vera is a 24-year-old **mechanical engineer** doing a master's in manufacturing, living with her parents above their repair shop.
She never uses AI tools, wants **traceable working** before she trusts anything, and sits in the political middle.
Her fear is local: factory closures, a **job near home**, and parents who depend on her.
In fast scenarios she turns to **hands-on** safety: maintenance, commissioning and keeping the robots running.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have no job or record when desk work goes.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **training**, firms that keep hiring graduates, and clear information on which jobs last.
